snippets.snippet_text: The Hebrew word for 'forgive' (salach) appears uniquely in scripture only with God as subject—it describes a forgiving that goes beyond human capacity, a divine act of erasure and restoration that deals with sin not proportionally but with overwhelming mercy.

Psalm 102:26 is radically mistranslated in the KJV. The Covenant Rendering reveals the true force: God laid the earth's foundation 'long ago,' establishing divine authority through that foundational act—a principle mirrored in the temple endowment's recitation of creation.

When God swears an oath in Psalm 110:4 ('The LORD hath sworn, and will not repent'), He binds Himself with the most solemn covenant commitment imaginable—establishing the Messiah's priesthood in the order of Melchizedek, the same order through which Latter-day Saint temple ordinances are performed.

The distance between east and west in Psalm 103:12 is infinite—unlike north and south, which have fixed endpoints. This spatial metaphor describes a separation so complete and inexhaustible that God's removal of our transgressions becomes incomprehensible to the human mind.

Psalm 116:15 declares that 'the death of his saints is precious in the sight of the LORD'—not because God enjoys suffering, but because the faithful who keep covenants become of immeasurable worth, and their commitment unto death demonstrates the weight of their devotion.

In Psalm 102:19–23, the suffering psalmist's personal testimony becomes cosmic: God records it 'for a generation to come,' and all peoples and kingdoms will eventually gather to worship—transforming private anguish into eschatological witness, directly paralleling D&C 110's vision of all nations gathering to the temple.
